transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Um... hi. I guess I'm here because... well, I'm just having a lot of trouble keeping things straight right now. Between my schoolwork and this little accessories shop I run, it's just... a lot. My supplies, the receipts, due dates for class, my notes... they all just sort of end up in these big piles. And I just sit there and I don't even know where to start.

How long have you been experiencing this difficulty with organizing things and getting started on tasks? Has this always been something you've struggled with, or is this something new that's started more recently?

Um... I guess it hasn't always been this bad. It's been a real problem for... maybe two years? Two years and two months, around there. It mostly started getting worse when I changed schools. I had to start managing the new business program and my shop at the same time, and... I don't know, there's just a lot less structure now. So... yeah. About that long.
When you sit down to work on something, like your schoolwork or shop tasks, do you find it hard to keep your attention on it, or do you start okay but then your mind wanders or you get distracted?

Um... yeah, I guess my mind wanders. Like... if I'm in class, or watching one of those videos for my business assignments, I can start out okay. I'm listening. But then... maybe a few minutes later, I'm thinking about charm designs or... ideas for shop orders. And then I realize I just missed half of what they said. So... yeah. It's hard to stay on it.

Before you changed schools two years ago, when you were younger, do you remember having trouble paying attention or staying organized in elementary or middle school? Or is this really something that only started when things got more complicated?

Um... I don't know. I guess there were things. 

Like... my mom still has these notes from my teachers in elementary school. They said I was... always getting up out of my seat, or blurting things out before they called on me. And... I guess I rushed through group stuff a lot, even if I knew how to do the work. 

So... yeah. I guess it was kind of there.

You mentioned trouble focusing in class and at work. How about at home or in other situations—do you find it hard to concentrate there too, or is it mainly when you're doing schoolwork and shop tasks?

Um... I'm not really sure. I haven't really noticed it much at home. 

I guess it's mostly just... when I have to sit down and do the school or shop stuff. I haven't really paid attention to it other times. So... yeah. I don't really know.

When you were in elementary school, say around ages 6 to 11, did your teachers or parents notice that you were fidgety, restless, or had trouble sitting still—not just during lessons, but regularly throughout the day?

Um... I don't really remember. 

I mean, I already said about the teacher notes and getting out of my seat in class, but... I don't know about the rest of the day. My parents didn't really say much about it to me. So... yeah. I'm not sure.
When you're doing things you really enjoy—like working on your shop designs or hobbies—do you find it easier to concentrate and stay focused, or do you still have trouble paying attention even then?

Um... I guess if it's something I really like doing... it's fine. 

I don't really think about it when I'm just doing my own stuff. It's just... normal, I guess. So, no, I don't really have trouble then. Just the other stuff.

When you're just hanging out with friends or doing everyday things like eating meals or watching TV, do you notice yourself feeling restless or fidgety, like you need to move around or can't sit still?

Um... I don't really know. I don't think so.

When I'm just hanging out or eating... I'm just doing that. I haven't really noticed feeling like I need to get up or anything. It's just... normal stuff. So, I don't think I do that.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a longstanding history of inattention and impulsivity dating back to elementary school (teacher notes documenting blurting out, getting out of seat, rushing through work), with current exacerbation over the past 2 years coinciding with increased environmental demands. While the acute worsening is situationally related to school/work transitions, the childhood-onset pattern of inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, combined with current difficulty sustaining attention and organizing tasks, is most consistent with ADHD, Combined or Predominantly Inattentive Type. The lack of current hyperactivity symptoms and situational nature of difficulties raise consideration of adjustment-related factors, but the developmental history and pervasive nature across multiple domains (school, work) support ADHD diagnosis.
